title: Cities, Resources and the Environment
bigQuestion: How do people organize cities, feed themselves, draw on the Earth, and divide it up, and can they keep doing so?

story.title: The View from the Top
story.kicker: From the 103rd floor of the Willis Tower, on a clear day, you can read a century and a half of human geography in the lines below.
paragraphs: The Willis Tower, finished in 1973 and called the Sears Tower for its first thirty-six years, rises 1,451 feet above Wacker Drive. Its skydeck sits on the 103rd floor. On a clear morning you can see four states: Illinois beneath you, Indiana to the southeast, and, on the very best days, the low shores of Michigan and Wisconsin across the water. But the most interesting view is straight down.

Start with the water. Lake Michigan fills the whole eastern horizon, the reason there is a city here at all. The Chicago River runs below you, and if you know what to look for you can see that it flows the wrong way. In 1900 engineers finished a canal that reversed it, so that Chicago's sewage would drain toward the Mississippi rather than into the lake that supplies the city's drinking water. Follow the river's South Branch and the Sanitary and Ship Canal beside it and you are tracing a highway for barges toward the Illinois River, the Mississippi, and the Gulf.

Now look for the rail lines. They come in from every direction and converge just south and west of the Loop, a knot of steel that was, and still is, the busiest rail hub in North America. In 1865 the Union Stock Yards opened at the end of those lines, and for a century cattle from the Plains and hogs from the corn belt arrived here to be turned into meat. The yards closed in 1971. The rails stayed, and now they carry containers from the Pacific coast bound for the East.

Look further out and the city sorts itself into rings and wedges. Office towers cluster in the Loop. Older factories and warehouses line the river and the rail corridors. Beyond them lie neighborhood after neighborhood of bungalows and two-flats, then the suburbs stretching to the horizon, then, past the edge of what you can see, the corn and soybean fields of the flattest, richest farmland in the world. A geographer named Ernest Burgess stood roughly here, in his imagination, in 1925 and drew this city as a set of concentric circles. His drawing became the first modern model of how cities grow.

Every topic in this chapter is visible from this deck: why cities form where they do and how they are laid out, how the farms beyond feed them, how factories rise and move away, where energy and water come from, what the smoke and the reversed river cost, and where the lines fall that make one side Illinois and the other Indiana. Chicago is not the whole story of human geography. But it is a remarkably complete chapter of it.
story.think: The river reversal solved Chicago's drinking-water problem by sending its waste toward towns downstream. Who paid the cost of that solution, and did they get a say?

lessons.title: Why Cities Grow Where They Do
lessons.mainIdea: More than half of humanity now lives in cities, and cities grow at sites where transportation routes, resources and markets meet.
reading: In 1800 about three percent of the world's people lived in cities. Around 2007 the share passed fifty percent, and by 2050 the United Nations expects it to reach about two-thirds. This shift from countryside to city is called *urbanization*, and it is one of the largest changes in human history. It is not finished. Most of the growth now is in Asia and Africa, where cities like Lagos, Dhaka and Kinshasa add hundreds of thousands of people a year, many of them arriving from villages with little more than a bag.

Cities grow where geography rewards them. Geographers speak of a city's *site*, the actual ground it sits on, and its *situation*, its position relative to other places and routes. Chicago's site was poor: a low, muddy plain that flooded. Its situation was superb. It sat at the one place where a short portage linked the Great Lakes water system to the Mississippi River system, so that a canoe, and later a canal boat, could pass from the Atlantic to the Gulf of Mexico. When railroads came in the 1850s they aimed at the same spot for the same reason.

The numbers show what a good situation is worth. In 1840 Chicago had about 4,500 people. By 1870 it had nearly 300,000. By 1900 it had 1.7 million, and it was the second-largest city in the country. No other city in the world had ever grown that fast for that long. Grain from the prairies, lumber from Wisconsin, cattle from the Plains and immigrants from Europe all passed through the same funnel, and each of them left a little behind.

Cities also arrange themselves into a hierarchy. A small town has a grocery store and a gas station. A county seat adds a hospital and a courthouse. A regional city adds a university and an airport. A few *world cities*, such as New York, London, Tokyo and, on most lists, Chicago, hold headquarters, financial markets and connections that serve the whole planet. The bigger the city, the rarer and more specialized the services it can support, and the wider the area it draws from.

words.d: the growth in the share of people living in cities rather than the countryside
the physical ground a city is built on, such as a harbor, a hill or a floodplain
a city's location relative to other places, routes and resources
a city whose finance, headquarters and connections serve the entire globe

look.title: Share of the World Living in Cities
look.cite: United Nations, rounded; 2050 is a projection
look.prompt: Between 1950 and 2050 the world's urban share more than doubles while its total population more than triples. About how many more city dwellers is that, roughly, and what do they all need?

check.q: What is the difference between a city's site and its situation?
choices: Site is its population; situation is its area
Site is the ground it sits on; situation is its position relative to other places
Site is its climate; situation is its government
They are two words for the same thing
check.why: Chicago's site was a muddy plain but its situation, at the link between two great water systems, made it grow.

check.q: Why did Chicago grow so fast in the 1800s?
choices: It had gold mines nearby
It was the national capital
It sat where the Great Lakes and Mississippi systems could be linked, and railroads followed
It had the best harbor on the Atlantic
check.why: The portage and later the canal and rail lines made Chicago the funnel for grain, lumber, cattle and immigrants.

check.q: Where is most urban growth happening today?
choices: In Europe and North America
In Asia and Africa
In Australia
In the Chicago suburbs
check.why: The reading names Lagos, Dhaka and Kinshasa as examples of cities adding hundreds of thousands of people a year.

lessons.title: Models of the City
lessons.mainIdea: Geographers use simple models, rings, wedges and multiple centers, to explain how land use sorts itself inside a city.
reading: In 1925 Ernest Burgess, a sociologist at the University of Chicago, drew the city as a bull's-eye. At the center was the business district, the Loop. Around it lay a zone of factories and cheap housing where new immigrants first landed. Beyond that came a ring of working-class homes, then a ring of better houses, then a commuter zone of suburbs. As the city grew, each ring pushed outward into the next. This *concentric zone model* was the first attempt to explain the shape of a city rather than just describe it.

Burgess had drawn Chicago, and Chicago is not every city. In 1939 the economist Homer Hoyt, using data on rents in many American cities, argued that land use grows in wedges, or sectors, along transportation lines rather than in rings. Factories follow a rail line or a river outward; wealthy neighborhoods extend along a lakefront or a scenic ridge. Chicago fits this too: industry spread southwest along the river and canal, and wealth spread north along the lake. In 1945 Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman added a third idea, the multiple nuclei model, in which a city has several centers, such as an airport, a university, a port and a mall district, each pulling its own kind of activity.

None of the three is simply right. They are tools for asking why a neighborhood is where it is. Cities outside the United States often follow other patterns. In many Latin American cities the rich live near the center along a grand avenue and the poorest live in self-built settlements on the edge, the reverse of the American pattern. Many European cities keep their historic core, protect it with strict rules, and push tall buildings to the outskirts.

Two forces have reshaped American cities since Burgess drew his circles. *Suburbanization* after 1945, powered by cars, highways and federal home loans, moved millions of families outward. Chicago's population peaked at about 3.6 million in 1950 and stands at about 2.7 million today, while its suburbs grew to hold more than twice that. More recently, *gentrification* has reversed the flow in some neighborhoods, as wealthier residents move into older areas near downtown, raising rents and pushing out long-time residents. Both processes are visible from the Willis Tower, one in every direction.

words.d: Burgess's 1925 model of a city as rings around a central business district
the movement of people and jobs from a central city to surrounding suburbs
the arrival of wealthier residents in an older, lower-income neighborhood, raising rents and changing who lives there

look.title: Burgess Draws the Rings
look.text: Burgess described the typical city as a series of concentric circles: a central business district at the core; a zone in transition being invaded by business and light manufacture; a zone of workers' homes for those who escaped the transition zone but want to live near work; a residential zone of better apartments and single homes; and, beyond the city limits, a commuters' zone.
look.cite: Ernest W. Burgess, The Growth of the City, 1925 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Burgess wrote before expressways and shopping malls. Which ring does an outer suburban office park belong in, and does his model have a place for it?

check.q: In the concentric zone model, where did Burgess say new immigrants usually first lived?
choices: In the commuter zone
In the ring just outside the central business district
In the ring of better houses
Outside the city entirely
check.why: The zone of factories and cheap housing around the Loop was where newcomers first landed before moving outward.

check.q: Hoyt's sector model differs from Burgess's model because it says land use grows in
choices: Wedges along transportation lines
Rings around the center
Random patches
A single line along the lake
check.why: Hoyt saw industry and wealth extending outward along rail lines, rivers and lakefronts, forming sectors instead of rings.

check.q: What happened to Chicago's population between 1950 and today?
choices: It doubled
It stayed about the same
It fell by roughly a quarter as suburbs grew
It fell to under one million
check.why: The city went from about 3.6 million to about 2.7 million while its suburbs grew to more than twice its size.

lessons.title: Life in the Fast-Growing City
lessons.mainIdea: Rapid urbanization brings opportunity and severe strain, from housing and water to transport, and cities handle it very differently.
reading: A city that grows faster than it can build is a hard place to live. Chicago in the 1880s had tenements without running water, streets of mud, and epidemics of cholera and typhoid carried by its own sewage. Today the same story plays out in Lagos, Nairobi, Mumbai and Manila. About one billion people, roughly a quarter of all city dwellers on Earth, live in *informal settlements*: neighborhoods built by their residents on land they do not own, usually without paved streets, sewers, or legal power and water connections.

Informal settlements are not simply slums. They are where a migrant from the countryside can afford to live, where small businesses start, and where communities organize. Dharavi in Mumbai, one of the densest places on the planet, holds thousands of small workshops recycling plastic, tanning leather and sewing garments. The problems are real: fires, floods, disease, eviction, and children who walk past open drains to school. The solutions that work best usually give residents legal title to their homes and then bring in water, sanitation and roads, rather than bulldozing the neighborhood.

Transportation shapes every city's growth. Cities built around walking are compact and dense. Cities built around streetcars and subways, like Chicago's Loop and the neighborhoods along the L lines, stretch along the rails. Cities built around cars, like Houston or Phoenix, sprawl for dozens of miles at low density. Sprawl brings bigger houses and yards but longer commutes, more pavement, and more fuel burned per person. Chicago has all three patterns in layers, which is why a trip across the region can take ninety minutes.

Cities also concentrate both wealth and poverty. Chicago remains one of the most racially segregated cities in the United States, a legacy of the covenants, redlining and public housing decisions described in the last chapter. Life expectancy in the Streeterville neighborhood is about thirty years longer than in Englewood, nine miles south. Geographers map these gaps because a map makes an argument: where you live in a city is one of the strongest predictors of how long you will live.

words.d: a neighborhood built by its residents on land they do not legally own, usually without sewers, paved roads or legal utilities
low-density growth of a city outward across a wide area, usually built around cars
the practice, common from the 1930s, of refusing loans in neighborhoods marked on maps as risky, usually because Black families lived there

look.title: Two Neighborhoods, Nine Miles Apart
look.text: Picture two Chicago blocks. On the first, near the lake, there are a hospital, a grocery store, a park with a running path, and apartments where most residents have college degrees and health insurance. On the second, nine miles south, the nearest full grocery store is a bus ride away, two lots on the block are empty, and the clinic closed in 2019. The people on the first block live, on average, about thirty years longer.
look.prompt: Name three specific things on the first block that add years of life, and explain how each one works. Which would be cheapest to bring to the second block?

check.q: About how many people worldwide live in informal settlements?
choices: About one million
About one billion
About one hundred thousand
About half of all people on Earth
check.why: Roughly a billion people, about a quarter of all city dwellers, live in neighborhoods they built themselves on land they do not own.

check.q: According to the reading, what approach to informal settlements usually works best?
choices: Bulldozing them and moving residents to the countryside
Leaving them exactly as they are
Giving residents legal title and then adding water, sanitation and roads
Banning migration to cities
check.why: Legal ownership plus basic services lets residents invest in their homes, while clearance destroys the communities and businesses they built.

check.q: A city built mostly around cars is likely to have
choices: Very high density and short commutes
Low density, long commutes and more fuel burned per person
No suburbs
Fewer roads than a walking city
check.why: Car-based cities like Houston or Phoenix sprawl outward at low density, which lengthens trips and raises fuel use.

lessons.title: From Subsistence to Agribusiness
lessons.mainIdea: Farming ranges from families growing their own food to global corporations, and Illinois sits at the industrial end of that range.
reading: Most farmers in history grew food mainly to feed themselves. That is *subsistence agriculture*, and hundreds of millions of families in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia still practice it, on plots of a few acres, with hand tools or an ox, and no surplus to sell in a bad year. The opposite is *commercial agriculture*: growing crops or animals to sell. A single Illinois farm family may work two thousand acres with a combine guided by satellites and sell nearly everything it grows to buyers it will never meet.

The gap between the two has widened since the 1950s. The *Green Revolution*, led by the American scientist Norman Borlaug, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970, bred new high-yield wheat and rice and spread them across Mexico, India and Pakistan along with fertilizer and irrigation. Grain harvests in India more than doubled in a generation, and famines that had killed millions became rare. The costs came later: heavy fertilizer runoff, falling water tables where wells were overpumped, and small farmers who could not afford the new seeds and chemicals.

In rich countries farming has become *agribusiness*, an industry that stretches from seed companies and tractor makers through the farm to grain traders, food processors and supermarkets. Illinois is a case study. The state grows more soybeans than any other and trades with Iowa for first place in corn. Most of that corn never reaches a dinner plate as corn: it feeds hogs and cattle, becomes ethanol fuel, or is turned into sweeteners and starch. Chicago's Board of Trade, founded in 1848, set the prices for the world's grain for more than a century.

The geography of what grows where follows soil, climate and distance to market. Central Illinois has some of the deepest, blackest prairie soil on Earth, left by glaciers and ten thousand years of grass, so it grows corn and soybeans. Wisconsin, cooler and hillier, keeps dairy cows. California's valleys, with irrigation, grow the vegetables and fruit that ship across the country. Florida grows oranges because it rarely freezes. Each region specializes, and the trucks and trains connecting them are as much a part of agriculture as the fields.

words.d: farming mainly to feed the farmer's own family, with little left to sell
farming to sell crops or animals rather than to eat them
the spread of high-yield seeds, fertilizer and irrigation from the 1950s that greatly raised grain harvests in Asia and Latin America
farming run as a large industry linked to seed, chemical, machinery, trading and food companies

look.title: Where Illinois Corn Goes
look.cite: Illinois and U.S. Department of Agriculture reports, rough shares, vary by year
look.prompt: Most Illinois corn becomes fuel or animal feed rather than food for people. If a drought cut the harvest by a third, who would feel it first: drivers, meat buyers, or foreign buyers?

check.q: What is subsistence agriculture?
choices: Farming with satellite-guided machines
Farming mainly to feed one's own family
Farming only for export
Farming without any tools
check.why: Subsistence farmers grow food to eat, not primarily to sell, and usually have little surplus.

check.q: What was one cost of the Green Revolution mentioned in the reading?
choices: Grain harvests fell in India
Famines became more common
Water tables fell where wells were overpumped
Farmers stopped using fertilizer
check.why: New seeds needed irrigation and fertilizer, which led to overpumped wells and runoff, and priced out some small farmers.

check.q: Why does Florida grow oranges while central Illinois grows corn?
choices: Federal law assigns crops to states
Florida rarely freezes; Illinois has deep prairie soil suited to corn
Illinois is too far from any market
Oranges cannot be shipped by train
check.why: Climate and soil decide what grows where, and each region specializes in what it does best.

lessons.title: Industry and the Global Division of Labor
lessons.mainIdea: Factories locate where materials, labor, markets and transport line up, and since the 1970s much manufacturing has moved across the world in search of lower costs.
reading: A factory is a decision about geography. Where should it sit? The German economist Alfred Weber argued in 1909 that a plant should go where the total cost of moving raw materials in and finished goods out is lowest. If the raw material is heavy and loses weight in processing, like iron ore becoming steel, build near the ore or the coal. If the product is bulkier or more fragile than its inputs, like bottled soda, build near the customers. Chicago's steel mills rose on the southeast side of the city because ore from Minnesota came down the lakes by ship and coal came up from Illinois by rail, and the two met there.

For a century the map of industry was the map of coal and iron: the English Midlands, Germany's Ruhr, the American belt from Pittsburgh through Cleveland and Detroit to Chicago and Gary. Then, from the 1970s on, that map came apart. Cheaper shipping containers, better communications, and trade agreements let companies split production across countries. Design might happen in California, chips in Taiwan, assembly in China or Vietnam, customer service in the Philippines. Geographers call this the *global division of labor*. Each step goes where it is cheapest to do well.

The results were uneven. Consumers worldwide got cheaper goods, and hundreds of millions of people in China, South Korea and elsewhere moved out of poverty into factory jobs. But in the old industrial belt, now often called the *Rust Belt*, mills and plants closed. Chicago lost most of its steel jobs; the Wisconsin Steel plant shut in 1980 and U.S. Steel's South Works, once employing about twenty thousand, closed in 1992. Gary, Indiana, lost more than half its population. Whole neighborhoods built around a plant's paycheck emptied out.

Manufacturing has not vanished from Illinois, but it has changed. The state still makes machinery, food products, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, often in plants that use far fewer workers than before because of automation. Meanwhile Chicago's economy has shifted toward finance, law, health care, universities and logistics, the business of moving goods through the same rail yards that once fed the stockyards. Recent policy debates about tariffs, supply chains and bringing production home all turn on the same question Weber asked in 1909: where should the factory go?

words.d: the splitting of production across countries so that each stage happens where it is cheapest to do well
the old industrial region from Pennsylvania through Ohio, Michigan, Indiana and Illinois where many factories closed after the 1970s
the use of machines and computers to do work formerly done by people

look.title: One Phone, Many Countries
look.text: A phone in your pocket was likely designed in one country, its chips made in a second, its screen in a third, its battery in a fourth, assembled in a fifth, and sold to you by a company that owns none of those factories. The parts crossed oceans several times before you touched it. The workers at each stop earned wildly different wages for an hour of work.
look.prompt: Why might a company choose to split production this way instead of building everything in one place? What could go wrong with a chain that long?

check.q: According to Weber, a steel mill should be built near
choices: The customers who buy steel
The iron ore and coal it uses
The company headquarters
A university
check.why: Ore and coal are heavy and lose weight in processing, so moving them is costly, and the mill goes where they are or where they meet.

check.q: What allowed companies after the 1970s to split production across many countries?
choices: The end of shipping by sea
Cheaper container shipping, better communications and trade agreements
A shortage of workers in Asia
Laws requiring factories to move
check.why: Lower transport and communication costs made it practical to do each stage wherever it was cheapest.

check.q: Which was an effect of the global division of labor on the Rust Belt?
choices: Steel employment in Chicago grew
Gary, Indiana doubled in population
Many mills closed and neighborhoods around them emptied
Consumer goods became more expensive
check.why: Plants like South Works closed and cities like Gary lost more than half their people, even as consumers elsewhere got cheaper goods.

lessons.title: Measuring Development
lessons.mainIdea: Development is measured by income, health and education together, and every measure has strengths and blind spots.
reading: How do you compare the well-being of Norway and Niger? The oldest yardstick is *gross domestic product* per person: the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its population. By that measure Norway is among the richest countries on Earth, at roughly one hundred thousand dollars per person, and Niger among the poorest, at under one thousand. The United States sits near eighty thousand and India near two thousand five hundred. GDP per person is easy to compute and it tracks a great deal, from cars to hospitals.

But GDP misses things. It counts a dollar earned by a billionaire the same as a dollar earned by a farmer, so it says nothing about who gets the money. It ignores unpaid work at home. It counts pollution cleanup as production. And a country can be fairly rich and still leave many people sick and uneducated. In 1990 the United Nations began publishing the *Human Development Index*, which combines three things: income per person, life expectancy at birth, and years of schooling. Norway, Switzerland and Iceland usually rank near the top; Niger, Chad and South Sudan near the bottom.

The map of development has a shape. Rich countries cluster in North America, Europe, East Asia and Australia; the poorest cluster in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia. Older textbooks called these the developed and developing worlds, or the global North and South. Those labels blur a lot. China's income per person has risen roughly tenfold since 1990. Within the United States, life expectancy in some counties trails that of much poorer countries. Development is a spectrum, and it moves.

Geographers argue about why the gap exists. Some point to geography itself: tropical disease, poor soils, landlocked positions far from ports. Some point to history: colonial rule that drew borders, extracted resources and left weak institutions. Some point to present policy: corruption, war, trade rules, and debt. Most likely all three matter, in different mixes in different places. What the measures show clearly is that the gap can close. Life expectancy in Africa has risen by more than a decade since 1990, and the share of the world in extreme poverty has fallen from more than a third to under a tenth.

words.d: the total value of everything a country produces in a year; per person, it is divided by the population
a United Nations measure combining income, life expectancy and years of schooling
the average number of years a newborn is expected to live under current conditions

look.title: Three Countries, Three Measures
look.cite: United Nations Human Development Report, about 2022, rounded
look.prompt: The United States is richer per person than Norway on some measures, yet Norwegians live about six years longer. What might explain a rich country falling short on health?

check.q: What three things does the Human Development Index combine?
choices: Income, life expectancy and years of schooling
Land area, population and army size
Exports, imports and debt
Roads, factories and farms
check.why: The index was designed to add health and education to income so that development is not measured by money alone.

check.q: Which is a weakness of GDP per person as a measure?
choices: It is very hard to calculate
It says nothing about how income is divided among people
It only counts farms
It is published only every fifty years
check.why: GDP per person is an average, so a country can look prosperous while most of its people are poor.

check.q: Which statement about the development gap is supported by the reading?
choices: The gap has been the same for all of history
The gap is caused only by climate
The gap can close, as Africa's rising life expectancy shows
Rich countries never have poor regions
check.why: Life expectancy in Africa has risen by more than a decade since 1990 and extreme poverty has fallen sharply worldwide.

lessons.title: Powering the World
lessons.mainIdea: About four-fifths of the world's energy still comes from coal, oil and gas, and shifting that mix is the central resource question of this century.
reading: Every city, farm and factory in this chapter runs on energy, and most of it comes from the ground. Coal, oil and natural gas, the *fossil fuels*, supply roughly eighty percent of the world's energy. They are concentrated in a few places: oil in the Persian Gulf, Russia, Venezuela, and the United States, which has become the world's largest producer; coal in China, India, the United States and Australia; gas in Russia, Iran, Qatar and the United States. Where the fuel is, and who controls the routes it travels, has shaped wars and alliances for a century.

Fossil fuels are *nonrenewable*: the Earth made them over millions of years and will not make more on any human timescale. Renewable sources, sun, wind, water, and heat from the Earth, do not run out, and their cost has fallen sharply. Solar panels cost roughly a tenth of what they did in 2010. Wind and solar now supply more than ten percent of the world's electricity and are the fastest-growing sources. Nuclear power, which produces no carbon dioxide but leaves radioactive waste, supplies about ten percent of the world's electricity as well.

Illinois is unusual. It generates more electricity from nuclear plants than any other state, from reactors along the Illinois, Mississippi and Rock rivers and near the Wisconsin line. Coal, mined in the state's southern counties for two centuries, has fallen from most of Illinois's power to a small share. Wind turbines now line the flat farmland of central Illinois, where they stand among the corn. Drive from Chicago to Springfield and you pass through most of the energy story in three hours.

The trade-offs are real. Fossil fuels are dense, portable and reliable, and the world's cars, ships, planes and steel mills were built around them. They also produce carbon dioxide that warms the planet, and burning coal fouls the air; air pollution is estimated to cause millions of early deaths worldwide each year. Renewables are clean and increasingly cheap, but the sun sets and the wind drops, so they need storage or backup. Poorer countries argue they should not be asked to skip the cheap fuels that made rich countries rich. Every energy choice is a geography question: where is it, who needs it, and who bears the cost?

words.d: coal, oil or natural gas, formed from ancient plants and animals over millions of years
a resource that is not replaced on a human timescale once used
a resource such as sunlight, wind or flowing water that is naturally replenished

look.prompt: Wind and solar are the fastest-growing sources but still a small slice. What would have to change for them to reach a third of the total, and who would pay for it?

choices: About twenty percent
About half
About eighty percent
Nearly all of it
check.why: Coal, oil and gas together supply roughly four-fifths of world energy, though renewables are growing fast.

check.q: Why are fossil fuels called nonrenewable?
choices: Because they are too expensive to renew
Because the Earth formed them over millions of years and will not replace them on a human timescale
Because governments have banned them
Because they only exist in the Persian Gulf

check.q: What is unusual about Illinois's electricity?
choices: It comes almost entirely from coal
It generates more from nuclear plants than any other state
It has no wind turbines

check.why: Illinois leads the nation in nuclear generation, while coal's share has fallen and wind has grown across central farmland.

lessons.title: Water and Food Security
lessons.mainIdea: Fresh water and food are unevenly distributed, and securing them depends as much on politics and infrastructure as on rainfall.
reading: Only about two and a half percent of the Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice or deep underground. The Great Lakes hold roughly a fifth of the world's surface fresh water, which is why Chicago has never had to worry about running dry. Much of the world is not so lucky. Cape Town, South Africa, came within weeks of shutting off its taps in 2018. The Aral Sea in Central Asia, once the fourth-largest lake on Earth, has mostly vanished since the 1960s because the rivers that fed it were diverted to grow cotton.

About seventy percent of the fresh water people use goes to farming, not to homes. That is the link between water and food. India and the United States both pump groundwater faster than rain refills it; the Ogallala Aquifer under the Great Plains, which waters wheat and corn from South Dakota to Texas, is dropping year by year. When water runs short, food does too. *Food security* means that everyone has reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food. By that standard, roughly one person in eleven worldwide still goes hungry, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and mostly because of poverty and war rather than a global shortage.

The world grows enough food to feed everyone. The problem is who can get it. Famine today almost always happens where there is fighting: Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen. Farmers cannot plant, roads are cut, and aid cannot get through. Meanwhile about a third of the food produced worldwide is lost or wasted, in fields, in storage and in kitchens. Chicago's own food deserts, neighborhoods far from any full grocery store, are a small version of the same problem: the food exists, but distance and cost keep it out of reach.

Water is also a border issue. Rivers do not stop at lines on a map. Egypt depends almost entirely on the Nile, whose water comes from Ethiopia, which finished a huge dam upstream in the 2020s. Turkey's dams control much of the water reaching Syria and Iraq. India and Pakistan have shared the Indus under a treaty since 1960 despite wars between them. Even the Great Lakes are governed by an agreement among eight states and two Canadian provinces that limits how much water can be taken out of the basin. Who is upstream matters.

words.d: an underground layer of rock or sand that holds water and can be pumped through wells
reliable access for everyone to enough safe and nutritious food
a neighborhood where residents live far from any store selling fresh, affordable food

look.title: The Lake That Became a Desert
look.text: In 1960 the Aral Sea stretched across the border of two Soviet republics, with fishing towns on its shores and a catch that fed the region. Planners in Moscow diverted the two rivers feeding it to irrigate cotton fields. By the 2000s ships lay rusting on sand dozens of miles from any water, the fishing towns were dying, and salt and pesticide dust blew off the dry lakebed into people's lungs.
look.prompt: The cotton did grow, and sold. Was the trade worth it? Who decided, and who lived with the result?

check.q: Where does most of the fresh water people use go?
choices: Drinking and cooking
Farming
Factories
Swimming pools
check.why: About seventy percent of fresh water used by people irrigates crops, which ties water shortages directly to food.

check.q: According to the reading, why does famine happen today?
choices: Because the world does not grow enough food
Mostly because of war and poverty that keep food from people
Because farmers refuse to sell
Because of food waste in rich countries
check.why: The world produces enough; fighting cuts roads, stops planting and blocks aid, and poverty keeps food out of reach.

check.q: Why is the Nile a source of tension between Egypt and Ethiopia?
choices: Egypt is upstream and controls the flow
Ethiopia is upstream and has built a large dam on water Egypt depends on
The river dried up in 2020
The two countries share no border
check.why: Rivers ignore borders, and the country upstream, here Ethiopia, controls what reaches the one downstream.

lessons.title: Climate, Change and Sustainability
lessons.mainIdea: Human activity is warming the climate, the effects fall unevenly across the map, and sustainability means meeting needs now without wrecking the future.
reading: People have always changed the land: clearing forests, draining marshes, plowing prairie, damming rivers. Illinois once had about twenty-two million acres of tallgrass prairie; less than one hundredth of one percent survives. What is new is the scale. Since about 1850, burning fossil fuels has raised the amount of carbon dioxide in the air by roughly half, from about 280 parts per million to over 420. Carbon dioxide traps heat, and the Earth's average temperature has risen a little over one degree Celsius, about two degrees Fahrenheit. That is the measured record, from ice cores, thermometers and satellites.

A degree does not sound like much, but it is an average across the whole planet, and it is not spread evenly. The Arctic has warmed about three times faster than the globe. Sea level has risen roughly eight inches since 1900 and is rising faster now, which matters most for low, crowded places like Bangladesh, the Nile delta, Miami and small Pacific islands. Heavier rain falls in some regions and longer droughts hit others. In Illinois, spring rains have grown heavier, flooding fields and basements, while summers bring more days above ninety degrees.

The costs fall unevenly too. The countries that burned the most fuel over the past two centuries, the United States and Europe first, then China, are mostly better placed to cope. Many of the countries that burned the least, in Africa and South Asia, face the worst heat, drought and flooding with the fewest resources. This is why international climate talks are so hard: they are arguments about who should cut, who should pay, and who should be helped, and the evidence gives no easy answer.

*Sustainability* means meeting today's needs without leaving the next generation less to work with. Chicago has tried it in pieces: reversing the river in 1900 was not sustainable for the towns downstream, but the Deep Tunnel project, begun in the 1970s, now stores stormwater in more than one hundred miles of tunnels to keep sewage out of the lake. Green roofs cover City Hall. The Chicago River, once an open sewer, now has fish, kayaks and herons. None of that undoes the larger problem. But it shows that a city can change what it does to the land, and the water, once it decides to.

words.d: a gas released by burning fossil fuels that traps heat in the atmosphere
meeting present needs without reducing what future generations will have
a way of measuring a small share; 420 parts per million means 420 out of every million molecules of air

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air
look.cite: Ice-core records and NOAA Mauna Loa measurements, rounded
look.prompt: The rise between 1950 and 2020 is larger than the rise in the previous century. What happened to the world's population, cities and energy use in those same seventy years?

check.q: How do scientists know the amount of carbon dioxide in the air has risen since 1850?
choices: From guesses based on population
From ice cores, thermometers and direct measurement
From old newspapers
From the color of the sky
check.why: Air bubbles trapped in ice record the past, and instruments such as those at Mauna Loa measure the present.

check.q: Why does a one-degree average rise matter more in some places than others?
choices: Because warming is spread perfectly evenly
Because the Arctic warms faster and low coasts face rising seas
Because only rich countries are affected
Because Illinois is not affected at all
check.why: An average hides big local differences: the Arctic warms about three times faster and low, crowded coasts face rising water.

check.q: Which Chicago project is given as an example of a more sustainable approach to water?
choices: The reversal of the river in 1900
The Union Stock Yards
The Deep Tunnel stormwater system
The Willis Tower skydeck
check.why: Deep Tunnel stores storm runoff so that sewage stays out of Lake Michigan, unlike the 1900 reversal that pushed waste downstream.

lessons.title: States, Nations and Borders
lessons.mainIdea: A state is a territory with a government; a nation is a people; the two rarely match perfectly, and borders are drawn by history, not nature.
reading: In geography, a *state* is not Illinois. It is a country: a defined territory with a permanent population, a government, and recognition by other states. There are about 195 of them. A *nation* is something different: a group of people who share a sense of common identity, usually through language, history and culture, and who feel they belong together. When one nation fills one state, as in Japan or Iceland, geographers call it a nation-state. Most states are not like that. They hold several nations, or a nation is split across several states, or both.

Borders are where the map gets argued over. Some follow rivers or mountain ridges, like the Rio Grande between Texas and Mexico or the Pyrenees between France and Spain. Some are straight lines drawn on a map by people who never saw the ground, like most of the border between the United States and Canada west of the Great Lakes, which runs along the forty-ninth parallel for more than a thousand miles. Illinois's own eastern border was drawn at a longitude line in 1818, and its northern border was pushed north from the tip of Lake Michigan so the new state would have a lakeshore, which is why Chicago is in Illinois and not Wisconsin.

Borders also fall apart and get redrawn. Since 1990 the map has changed a great deal. The Soviet Union split into fifteen states in 1991. Yugoslavia broke into seven. Czechoslovakia divided peacefully in 1993. South Sudan became the newest widely recognized state in 2011 after decades of war. Elsewhere borders are frozen in dispute: Kashmir between India and Pakistan since 1947, the line dividing Korea since 1953, and the borders of Israel and the Palestinian territories.

Inside a state, lines matter too. The United States divides power between the national government and fifty states, a system called federalism, and each state divides itself again into counties, cities, townships and districts. Illinois has 102 counties. Chicago has fifty wards, each electing an alderperson, and the lines of those wards are redrawn after every census. Where a line falls decides which school a child attends, which police respond, who collects the taxes and who gets to vote for whom. Political geography is the study of how those lines are drawn and what they do.

words.d: in geography, a country: a territory with a permanent population, a government and recognition by other countries
a people who share a common identity through language, history or culture
a state whose population is mostly one nation, such as Japan or Iceland
a system that divides power between a national government and regional governments such as the fifty U.S. states

look.title: The Constitution Counts Everyone
look.text: The actual Enumeration shall be made within three Years after the first Meeting of the Congress of the United States, and within every subsequent Term of ten Years, in such Manner as they shall by Law direct.
look.cite: United States Constitution, Article I, Section 2, 1787
look.prompt: This clause created the census. Why would a government that draws district lines and shares out seats in Congress need to count everyone every ten years?

check.q: In geography, what is the difference between a state and a nation?
choices: A state is a people; a nation is a territory with a government
A state is a territory with a government; a nation is a people with a shared identity
They are the same thing
A state is always smaller than a nation
check.why: Japan is both a state and a nation; the Kurds are a nation without a state; most states contain several nations.

check.q: Why is Chicago in Illinois rather than Wisconsin?
choices: Wisconsin gave the land away in 1900
Illinois's northern border was moved north in 1818 to give the state a lakeshore
The Chicago River marks the state line
Chicago voted to join Illinois
check.why: The 1818 border was pushed north from the tip of Lake Michigan so the new state would touch the lake.

check.q: Which of these borders is an example of one drawn as a straight line on a map rather than along a natural feature?
choices: The Rio Grande between Texas and Mexico
The Pyrenees between France and Spain
The forty-ninth parallel between the United States and Canada
The Mississippi between Illinois and Missouri
check.why: The forty-ninth parallel is a line of latitude chosen on a map; the other three follow rivers or mountains.

lessons.title: Conflict and Cooperation Across Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Borders create conflict over land, people and resources, but states also cooperate through treaties, alliances and shared rules.
reading: Lines on a map create both problems and solutions. Conflicts over borders come in a few familiar types. Some are about where the line is, like the disputed ridges between India and China. Some are about what the line cuts through: a nation split in two, a river shared, an oil field beneath both sides. Some are about who is inside it, when a group within a state wants its own, as in Catalonia in Spain, Scotland in the United Kingdom, or Quebec in Canada, each of which has voted on leaving. And some are about lines that no longer exist but that people remember.

The forces that pull a state together are called *centripetal*: a shared language, a national story, a strong economy, fair institutions, a common threat from outside. The forces that pull it apart are *centrifugal*: regional inequality, ethnic or religious division, a government that favors one group, geography that isolates a region. Every state has both. The United States survived a civil war over its own dividing line and has argued ever since about how much power should sit in Washington and how much in the states.

States also cooperate, because most problems cross borders. The United Nations, founded in 1945, gives every recognized state a seat and a place to argue instead of fight, though its Security Council can act only when its five permanent members agree. The European Union has turned twenty-seven states into a single market with open internal borders. Trade agreements like the one linking the United States, Mexico and Canada set rules for goods that cross their lines. The Great Lakes agreement among eight states and two provinces is a smaller version of the same thing: shared water, shared rules.

Chicago lives on both sides of this. It is a global city whose airport connects it to every continent, whose grain and machinery cross oceans, and whose neighborhoods hold people from more than a hundred countries. It is also a city where ward lines, school boundaries and the state line with Indiana decide who pays for what. Human geography ends where it began, with a question: where should the lines go, and who gets to decide?

words.d: something that unites a state, such as a shared language or fair institutions
something that divides a state, such as regional inequality or ethnic conflict
the organization founded in 1945 in which almost every state has a seat to negotiate and cooperate

look.title: A Vote to Leave
look.text: In 2014 the people of Scotland voted on whether to leave the United Kingdom and become an independent state. The campaign argued over currency, oil in the North Sea, pensions, borders, language and history. Roughly fifty-five percent voted to stay. Similar votes have been held or demanded in Quebec and Catalonia, with different results and different reactions from the national governments.
look.prompt: List the centripetal and centrifugal forces at work in a vote like this. Why might a national government allow such a vote in one case and forbid it in another?

check.q: Which is an example of a centrifugal force?
choices: A shared national language
Fair courts that treat everyone alike
Deep regional inequality that leaves one area feeling ignored
A common threat from a neighboring country
check.why: Centrifugal forces pull a state apart. The other three tend to hold a state together.

check.q: Why can the United Nations Security Council sometimes fail to act?
choices: It has no members
It meets only once a decade
It can act only when its five permanent members agree
It has no building
check.why: Any one of the five permanent members can block action, so agreement among them is required.

check.q: What has the European Union done for its member states?
choices: Made them into one country with one language
Created a single market with open internal borders
Abolished all their governments
Closed their borders to trade
check.why: The EU keeps its members as separate states but lets goods and people move freely among them.

review.q: Around what year did more than half the world's people come to live in cities?
review.why: The urban share passed fifty percent around 2007 and is projected to reach about two-thirds by 2050.

review.q: Which model describes a city as growing in wedges along transportation lines?
choices: Burgess's concentric zone model
Hoyt's sector model
The multiple nuclei model
The demographic transition model
review.why: Hoyt argued in 1939 that industry and wealth extend outward along rail lines, rivers and lakefronts.

review.q: What was a main achievement of the Green Revolution?
choices: It ended the use of fertilizer
It more than doubled grain harvests in countries like India
It moved farming from Illinois to California
It created the Chicago Board of Trade
review.why: High-yield seeds with fertilizer and irrigation raised harvests sharply and made famine rare in Asia.

review.q: Why did Chicago's steel mills locate on the city's southeast side?
choices: Ore came down the lakes by ship and coal came up by rail, meeting there
The land was the most expensive in the city
The mills needed to be far from any water
Federal law required it
review.why: As Weber's theory predicts, heavy raw materials drew the mills to the place where ore and coal met.

review.q: The Human Development Index improves on GDP per person by adding
choices: Military strength
Life expectancy and years of schooling
Land area
The number of cities
review.why: The index combines income with health and education so development is not measured by money alone.

review.q: Which state generates more electricity from nuclear plants than any other?
choices: Texas
California
Illinois
Florida

review.q: Which statement about world hunger is supported by the chapter?
choices: The world does not grow enough food for everyone
Famine today almost always happens where there is war
Hunger is spread evenly across all countries
Food waste is under one percent of production

choices: A state without a nation
A nation without a state
A nation-state
A federal district
